rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$V\propto n\ \text{at constant }T,P;\qquad \frac{V_{1}}{n_{1}}=\frac{V_{2}}{n_{2}}$$
$$M=2\times VD\ (\text{H}_{2}\ \text{reference});\qquad M=28.94\times VD\ (\text{air reference})$$
$$n=\frac{V\ (\text{STP})}{22.4\ \text{L}},\qquad n=\frac{N}{N_{A}},\qquad V_{\text{molar}}=22.4\ \text{L at STP}$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Equal volumes of any two gases have equal masses. ✅ They have equal *numbers of molecules*; masses differ because molecular masses differ.  ·  ❌ Vapour density is the same as density. ✅ Vapour density is a *relative* quantity measured with respect to hydrogen (or air); density is an absolute mass per unit volume.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Avogadro number N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ (exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ since the 2019 SI revision).  ·  Molar volume: 22.4 L at STP (0 °C, 1 atm) and 24.0 L at RTP (25 °C, 1 bar).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** VD of a gas is 22; find its molar mass and the mass of 5.6 L at STP. **Solution:** M = 2 × 22 = 44 g mol⁻¹; n = 5.6/22.4 = 0.25 mol → mass = 0.25 × 44 = 11 g.  ·  **Problem:** Calculate the number of molecules in 11.2 L of CH₄ at STP and the number of hydrogen atoms present. **Solution:** n = 11.2/22.4 = 0.5 mol → molecules = 0.5 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³; H atoms = 4 × that = 1.204 × 10²⁴.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: avogadro's law, some deductions: molecular mass, vapour density, molecular mass (within Stoichiometry).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning and statement  ·  Avogadro's law (Amedeo Avogadro, 1811, published as a hypothesis) states: equal volumes of all gases, under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules. Hence for a gas $V\propto n$ at constant T and P, and volume ratio = mole ratio.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Avogadro's hypothesis (1811) was accepted only after Cannizzaro (1858) explained it, and one mole of water is just 18 mL of liquid — yet it contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.  ·  1 mole = 6.022×10²³ entities (Avogadro constant, Nₐ). Molar mass (M) is g·mol⁻¹; for a compound M = Σ(atomic masses).

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Deduction 1 — molecular mass and vapour density  ·  **Vapour density (VD)** of a gas is the ratio of the mass of a certain volume of the gas to the mass of the same volume of hydrogen under identical conditions. Because equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules, masses are in the ratio of molecular masses, and with hydrogen as the standard (M = 2): $VD=\frac{M}{2}$, so **molecular mass = 2 × vapour density**.…  ·  ### 3. Deduction 2 — molecular mass and volume of gas

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: n = m / M  ·  n = V / 22.4 (g at STP)  ·  % yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • Volume of gas  ·  ❌ 1 mole of every gas occupies 22.4 L under all conditions. ✅ Only at STP (273.15 K, 1 atm); at other conditions use PV = nRT.  ·  ❌ Molecular mass equals vapour density. ✅ Molecular mass = 2 × vapour density (for the hydrogen reference).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Avogadro's law can be applied to a dissociating gas without correction. ✅ Dissociation/association changes the number of particles, so an apparent (abnormal) vapour density results.  ·  ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ entities (avogadro constant, nₐ). molar mass (m) is g·mol⁻¹; for a compound m = σ(atomic masses)..  ·  Remember the abnormal vapour density correction for dissociating gases such as PCl₅ and N₂O₄.

rows.text: State Avogadro's law and deduce the relation between molecular mass and vapour density.  ·  Show that the mass of 22.4 L of any gas at STP equals its molar mass in grams.  ·  Calculate the molecular mass of a gas whose vapour density is 30.

rows.text: The vapour density of an oxide of nitrogen is 46; find its molecular formula if it contains 30.4% nitrogen.  ·  Explain how Avogadro's law established that hydrogen and oxygen are diatomic.  ·  State the limitations of Avogadro's law.
